archs.name: arch-static-hybrid (Design A: static hybrid retrieval, zero server, zero per-query cost)
archs.summary:
Complete Design A, about 1,000 lines with 27 plan items (arch-static-hybrid-01 to 27). A build pipeline turns public-domain sources and the site's own JSON into immutable, content-hashed, lazily loaded tiers. T1 is a small entity, facts and lexicon tier (units at every echelon, people, places, tenures, stats with authority, roll-ups, time anchors, known-unknowns). T2 is a sharded passage tier (BM25 impact postings in 128 hash buckets plus 16-passage text shards). T3 is optional roster shards and T4 is media. A Web Worker links entities, classifies intent, answers who/when/where/how-many questions directly from tables, and answers narrative questions with verbatim, page-cited passages. Every quote is span-validated at build and in CI. Nothing is generated, so the composer cannot fabricate a sentence; it can still select a wrong passage, which the eval measures. The report covers the data model (source, document, passage, entity, fact, anchor and manifest schemas), a 12-stage ingestion pipeline with a human review queue, hosting/service-worker/header layout, retrieval and ranking, 14 answer types, UI/UX, a 150-question golden set with metrics and gates, governance, budgets, phased delivery, 20 risks, and dependencies.

Measured for this design on the seven public-domain sources already local (OR Ser. I vol. 27 Pts 1-3, NY Final Report v1, Fox, Battles & Leaders v3, Joint Committee v1), using scripts in plan-work/tmp-arch-static-hybrid/:
- **Corpus:** 3.19 M words, 14,391 passages, 16.2 MB of text. That is 288x the 11,088 words the Historian indexes today.
- **Index and text size:** the full inverted index is 1.5 MB brotli (128 shards, 12 KB average, 20 KB maximum). Text as 16-passage shards is 5.7 KB each (367 B per passage). The lexicon is 34 KB. The 957-record entity tier is 76 KB. Extrapolated to 40,000 passages the lazy total is about 30-36 MB including rosters, inside the 40 MB budget.
- **Latency:** decode, BM25 and top-10 take 0.057 ms p50 and 0.126 ms p95 in Node. Fuzzy repair takes 3.5 ms. Modelled worker compute on a phone is about 50-60 ms unoptimised, with a 50 ms target. Phone timings are a x6 model, not a device run.
- **Typo repair:** Damerau-Levenshtein reached 100% recall on 2,682 synthetic single-edit typos with about 1.05 candidates. Soundex reached 34-100% and a consonant-skeleton key 11-99%, so DL is primary and Soundex is dropped.
- **Unit linking:** a naive alias regexp was wrong on 7 of 22 sampled links (compound ordinals, arm confusion). A grammar linker with arm agreement linked 24.1% of 6,332 OR/NY passages, 3,820 confident mentions, and 389 of 467 site regiment records (83%). Today 9.6% of regiments are mentioned anywhere. The manual sample was only 25 items, so this is illustrative, not a precision estimate.
- **Time evidence:** there are 5,702 clock expressions but only 75 sentences with both a place term and a clock time. Anchors therefore attach at report/unit/day level and are stored as 1863 clock minutes, never ticks, so the pending time-model fix (audit C4) cannot invalidate the KB.
- **Other:** 0.6% near-duplicate passages, and 1.4-10.6% of passages are table-like and need a classifier stage.

Not verified: WebFetch and WebSearch hit a spend limit, so no third-party library or platform documentation was re-read. Pagefind, MiniSearch and Orama facts, Netlify file-count limits, whether the CDN compresses `.bin` files, HTTP Range support, and the Netlify plan tier are all marked [U]. Four Phase-0 spikes (S-1 to S-4) are specified to settle them. Total effort is about 54-85 person-days [E].

archs.name: arch-semantic-local (Design B: on-device semantic layer)
archs.summary:
Design B is an opt-in, on-device dense-retrieval layer on top of Design A. Passage embeddings are precomputed offline and the query is embedded in the visitor's browser (ONNX Runtime Web, single-thread WASM, in a Worker). It is fused with A's lexical/entity channel by weighted RRF and gated by a calibrated answer/partial/decline decision. Answers are extractive only: quoted spans with page-level citations, perspective chips and licence lines. No query, embedding or click leaves the device, and T0 (A alone) stays the default and the fallback.

The report is 1,154 lines. It covers goals, the chunk/record schema, binary vector and column formats, a 12-stage ingestion pipeline, hosting and CDN layout, the retrieval algorithm, answer composition, UI/UX, the evaluation plan, governance, budgets, phases, 28 risks and 31 findings.

What I measured or verified:
- **Headroom on today's corpus is small.** Of the 23 strict failures left in the A prototype (175 queries), only 6 (3.4% of the battery) are assistable by semantic matching: 5 scope/decline cases and 1 typo. So B is justified only by the expanded prose corpus.
- **Real chunk counts.** The Official Records Vol. 27 Pts 1-3 give 11,425 chunks (9,483 narrative, 83%). About 28% of chunks contain a clock time and 35.5% mention a numbered unit.
- **Vocabulary-gap pilot.** A 33-question BM25 pilot on those chunks (single author, caveats in the report) gives recall@5 of 100% for source-vocabulary phrasing, 66.7% for keyword phrasing and 27.3% for plain-language questions. For plain questions, 24% get the answer in the top 3, 48.5% get only related chunks, and 27% get nothing related. A lexical-only gate would still answer that last group.
- **Brute-force scan is enough.** On a Core Ultra 7 desktop, a 50k x 384 int8 scan takes 11.0 ms and a binary prefilter takes 0.8 ms. No HNSW/IVF is needed up to at least 200k vectors.
- **Models.** Snowflake arctic-embed-xs is the default (Apache-2.0, 22.6M params, 6 layers, MTEB retrieval 50.15, int8 ONNX 22.97 MB). bge-small-en-v1.5 (MIT, 51.68, about 34 MB) is the quality alternative. A B0 bake-off picks the smallest model that is not significantly worse than the best.
- **Static-embedding tier.** Model2Vec potion static models score 32.7-35.1 on retrieval, so they are fallback or optional only.
- **Runtime sizes.** onnxruntime-web 1.30.0: 3.07 MB brotli for the WASM, 5.48 MB brotli for the WebGPU build. The WebGPU build is reserved for the optional reranker.
- **Platform facts.** Netlify serves Range/206 and brotli. WebKit deletes script-writable storage, including caches, after 7 days of Safari use without interaction. Safari's browser-app origin quota is up to 60% of disk. WebGPU is available in iOS Safari 26+ only.
- **Two blocking bugs in the current sw.js.** Its activate handler deletes every cache not named CACHE_NAME (lines 24-31), which would wipe the Historian's 40 MB cache on each update. Its /data/ handler caches every response (lines 58-70). The plan patches both before any Historian cache exists.

Not run: no neural embedding, because I had no approval to download model weights and no ML stack is installed. Every dense-retrieval quality claim is a design target, and B0 turns them into results. Phone latencies are estimates.

Decisions built into the plan:
- **Kill criterion.** If hybrid does not beat BM25-only by at least +10 recall@5 points on the paraphrase subset (95% CI excluding 0), or misses the budgets, B stops. The fallback is A plus build-time doc2query expansion.
- **Golden set.** About 150 questions (30 entity/fact regression, 45 passage, 25 conceptual, 15 time-anchored, 10 contested, 25 refusal), with a frozen 50-question test split.
- **Time anchors.** Only source-stated times are stored, never rewritten to the site clock (audit C4).
- **Deep links.** They use #q= instead of ?q= so the question is never sent to the server.
- **No generative model on the device.** Revisit criteria are in section 5.6.
- **Tier-B and Tier-C sources.** Tier B (Wikipedia/OSM) stays out of the default vectors. Tier C is never fetched.
- **Open questions.** Ten decisions for the owner are listed in section 17.1.

archs.name: arch-rag-function
archs.summary:
Complete Design C for Ask the Historian, written to arch-rag-function.md (about 26k words, 17 sections plus 7 appendices). No Claude API call was made, so every latency and answer-quality figure is an estimate for the R0 spike to measure; costs are arithmetic on published prices.

Architecture: router-first RAG. A shared deterministic engine (the H1/H2 search-core from hist-current) runs in the browser and in a Netlify Function. It normalises the question, links entities, classifies intent and gates before any paid call. Each question takes one of seven routes: decline, deterministic facts, curated (human-reviewed) answer, cached AI answer, AI answer, AI with tools (R3), or a no-AI extractive answer. Roughly 40% of questions should never reach Claude (estimate from the 118-query battery).

Grounding and citations:
- Grounding has seven layers: pre-LLM gate, vetted corpus, frozen sources-only prompt, native citations, ten deterministic claim checks, sampled Haiku 4.5 verifier, extractive fallback, plus offline governance.
- Citations use Claude search_result blocks. The API returns cited_text and block indices verbatim; that text is not billed as output. Each chunk is stored as sentence blocks with character offsets and page/leaf locators, so a quote span resolves to a scan page.
- Citations are incompatible with structured outputs (API returns 400), so the composer output is free text.
- Claims reach the reader only after they pass the checks, so text appears claim by claim, not token by token.

Corpus and retrieval, measured on the real Official Records text: 79,723 sentences (mean 20.2 words), 5,417 clock-time expressions, 8,877 chunks of about 171 words. The OR-only lexical index is 0.87 MB compressed and the chunk text 2.8 MB compressed, so the full lexical index should fit in a function. On 20 probe questions with header-derived gold labels, plain BM25 found the right report in the top 5 for only 6/20; adding the report header as a weighted field gave 12/20. These probes used crude segmentation (523 of 589 headers found) and are directional only.

Model policy: Claude Opus 5.5 at effort low as reference and launch default, with Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 4.5 adopted per route only via a golden-set bake-off. Haiku 4.5 handles verifier and query rewrite. Server-side fallbacks are enabled, which requires the direct Anthropic API rather than Netlify AI Gateway (no header pass-through, 5-minute cache only).

Abuse and privacy:
- Cost controls: Netlify rateLimit, a self-hosted proof-of-work challenge (ALTCHA, MIT) instead of a third-party CAPTCHA, salted hashed-IP token buckets, per-day and per-month dollar budgets, a circuit breaker and kill switch, and Anthropic workspace spend caps as the authoritative backstop.
- The design flags two provider signals as budget exhausted: HTTP 429 without retry-after, and HTTP 400 "You have reached your specified API usage limits".
- Privacy: AI answers are opt-in with a first-use notice, no raw question logging, and required edits to the privacy page and banner (both currently promise no personal data and browser-only operation).

Honest positioning is a measurable contract: at least 98% of factual sentences carry a verified citation, unsupported numerals are 0 in CI, and each answer wears a badge.

Evaluation: a 150-question golden set (100 dev, 50 held-out, 13 categories, three runs each) with pooled gold labelling, judge calibration (kappa at least 0.8) and phase gates.

Other deliverables: 12 owner decisions with defaults, 31 work items, 22 risks, about 40 seed questions, the draft system prompt, and a function skeleton.

strengths: Runtime cost is $0 per query with no server, key or LLM. Per-session payload is about 0.35 MB, so bandwidth is small: 3,000 sessions/month is about 96 credits including 60 for four deploys, and 15,000 is about 238 (A section 12.3). Build-time spend is $0 in API fees.

No on-call surface. Everything is content-hashed, immutable static files, and the failure mode is 'stale', not 'down'. There is no runtime third-party dependency, so connect-src 'self' holds and the privacy page needs only one sentence.

Solo-maintainer burden is front-loaded and stoppable. Phases P0-P5 each have numeric gates, so the owner can stop at any tier and still ship (risk R11). The pipeline is deterministic and rerunnable, and the review queue has confidence valves so unreviewed links never drive structured answers.

The evidence is the strongest of the three because it was measured on real text: 14,391 passages (288x today's corpus), a 1.5 MB brotli index, p50 0.057 ms BM25, and a 34 KB lexicon. A grammar-based unit linker reached 24/25 correct where the naive alias linker was wrong 7 of 22 times.

Best time-to-value. P1 (about 10-14 d) fixes the current Historian on the site's own data with no licensing risk. P2 (8-12 d plus 8-15 h review) then adds page-cited Official Records answers and the time-evidence tables for audit C4.

The KB is architecture-neutral. Sentence-boundary offsets, entity ids and citation objects can carry a later LLM or dense tier without re-ingestion. It also spins off SEO-indexable regiment/entity pages (finding 25), which addresses audit T1 (only ~8% of referrals come from search).
Compact-fits-budget design: 0 bytes on first paint, T1 of 250 KB or less, cold passage query of 120 KB or less, and a lazy corpus of about 21-36 MB at 25-40k passages.
weaknesses: Largest up-front build: about 54-85 person-days (4-6 calendar months at about 15 h/week). This number covers the whole content pipeline, including source ingestion, so it is not directly comparable with B's 20-25 d or C's 26-38 d, which exclude the shared 45-80 d of ingestion.
The recurring human cost is the review queue (8-15 h for the OR backbone, then a few hours per source). It is unbounded (R11) and needs a 3-4 h/week budget plus ideally a named historian reviewer.

Gate re-tuning recurs with every data expansion. In the prototype, adding 299 records dropped canonical@1 from 91.4 to 87.9 and correct decline from 94.1 to 88.2 (A section 7.10, risk R13). The P1 exit gates were not reached on held-out data by the prototype (S@1 88.5, canonical@1 81.8, decline 40.0, n=5), so re-baselining is likely.

At 2.7k-3.5k files it forces Git/CLI deploys (also needed for N1). Netlify file-count limits, .bin compression and Range support are unverified ([U]) and gated on spikes S-1/S-2. Each production deploy costs 15 credits (infra-netlify.md:588), so 'corrections ship in a day' should be batched weekly, since 20 deploys equal the whole 300-credit Free allowance. That batching is my inference on the sourced 15-credit figure.
Lexical plus entity retrieval has a vocabulary-gap ceiling on paraphrase and multi-hop 'why' questions (A section 14, R7). It cannot synthesize.
It does not identify that deployed sw.js:24-31 deletes every cache not named CACHE_NAME. A's proposed hx-v<schema> cache would be wiped on the next service-worker bump. The fix is in B section 8.4.

Netlify plan tier and credit balance are unverified. infra-netlify.md:588 notes the 30-day RUM windows suggest Pro or a legacy plan, so the credit tables are conditional. WebFetch/WebSearch hit a spend limit mid-task, so no third-party library or platform docs were re-read.

scores.design: B: On-device semantic layer on top of A (arch-semantic-local.md)
strengths: No server, no API key, no per-query dollars, and no privacy-policy change, because queries and embeddings never leave the device. There is no abuse surface for the owner to police.

Well fenced against sunk cost. It is opt-in, adds zero bytes on first paint, and degrades T3 -> T2 -> T0+ -> T0 with a manifest kill switch. A 4-day B0 spike carries a kill criterion of +10 points recall@5 on 60+ paraphrase items with a CI excluding 0. If that fails, the fallback is the build-time T0+ expansion.

Sound engineering discipline: same-ONNX-file parity for index and query, tokenizer and embedding parity tests, model_id pinned by hash, and a paired-bootstrap power check (it honestly notes +5-point wins are not detectable at n about 95, CI about +/-11-13).

Best analysis of the service worker. It found that sw.js:24-31 purges every non-current cache, and that /data/ is cached network-first. Both bugs would silently destroy any large client cache, including A's.

T0+ build-time doc2query expansion (indexed-only, generated:true, never quoted) gives most visitors part of the semantic benefit at roughly zero runtime cost. Encoder and runtime choices are licence-clean (arctic-embed-xs Apache-2.0, 22.97 MB int8; ORT wasm 3.07 MB br) and were verified against primary pages.
weaknesses: Its value is unproven on today's corpus. On the current 175-query battery only 6 of 175 failures (3.4 points) are even assistable by semantic matching (B section 2.1). No neural embedding was actually run, so every dense-retrieval quality claim is a design target, not a result.

Bandwidth is the heaviest per user: an opt-in download of about 40 MB (about 27 MB model+runtime plus 13-21 MB vectors). At about 110 Historian views/30 d and 30% opt-in that is about 33 users/month (about 26 credits). At 10x traffic it is about 264 credits, 88% of the Free 300-credit hard limit. iOS 7-day eviction adds re-download cost, and a single scraper pulling 100 copies is about 80 credits.

High silent-failure maintenance surface for a solo dev: ORT 1.30.x and transformers.js 4.x churn (the v4 API was not verified, [U]), tokenizer and embedding parity CI, WebGPU fragmentation, per-page CSP with 'wasm-unsafe-eval', a client cache manager and eviction detection, and a real-device matrix that needs phones the owner may not have. Phone latencies are all estimates.

Not standalone. It needs A's interfaces I1-I8 (search-core, passage store, worker, time model, id crosswalk). It is only worth building after A's expanded corpus exists, and it still ends in extractive answers, never synthesis.

Core effort is 20-25 d (29-41 d with B4/B5, plus 3-5 d for B6), for a benefit that reaches roughly 33 opt-in users/month today. The 27% 'confidently wrong' pilot tail is a gate problem that A's scope-exemplar/gate work partly addresses at lower cost. Its pilot was single-author with gold in view, so it is directional.

Legal status of embeddings of share-alike text is unsettled, so Tier B stays out of the vectors. Netlify .wasm content-type and brotli behavior and the host alternatives (R2, GitHub Pages) were not verified.

scores.design: C: RAG serverless function calling Claude (arch-rag-function.md)
strengths: Only design that can compose narrative and 'why' answers with sentence-block citations that come verbatim from the API (cited_text, not typed by the model). It has seven grounding layers, a deterministic D1-D10 numeral/date/name check, and a fail-closed extractive fallback (S0).

Dollar exposure is bounded and small at today's scale. It is about $0.0235/answer on Opus 5.5 with a warm cache and about $0.012 on Sonnet 5.5. Monthly base cost is $14/$7 at 1k queries and $100/$53 at 10k. Launch caps are $25/month and $2/day, with an Anthropic workspace limit at $30 that is authoritative (D-02, B8). Prompt caching policy (off below about 300 calls/month, 1-hour TTL above) is worked out.

Availability does not depend on the provider. The Historian page answers D0/D1/S0 in the browser with the function off, and the state machine ON/SHED/STATIC/RECOVER plus a Blobs kill switch (about 15 s) is well specified.

Routing before the model means about 40% of questions never reach a paid call (E). Offline Batch-API use is cheap: about $50-100 one-time for ingestion assistance and about $6.5 for 400 pre-generated answers, and the design says human review is the real cost.

R1 (7-9 d plus the shared H1 engine) can ship over the site's own records with no third-party licensing risk. The privacy story (opt-in notice, no raw-question logging, salted rotating IP hashes) is thoughtful and includes the needed page rewrites (audit X5).
weaknesses: Highest ongoing operational burden of the three. It needs four functions (ask, health, challenge, feedback), six Netlify Blobs stores with last-write-wins approximate counters, a proof-of-work challenge, rate limits, a circuit breaker, an anomaly watcher, prompt versioning, a model bake-off, an LLM-judge golden set (kappa at least 0.8), an incident runbook (P0-P3), and quarterly accuracy reports. Its risk table lists 22 risks, several rated high impact.

Recurring cost has a floor independent of traffic: evals about $30-60/month plus canary about $10/month (C section 14.5), which exceeds serving cost at today's roughly 110 Historian views/30 d. Serving cost is then linear, about $100 per 10k queries on Opus. Effort is 26-38 d RAG-specific, on top of H1 (3-4 d) and shared ingestion (45-80 d).

Single-provider and platform dependencies: model deprecation and repricing, Anthropic key custody and rotation, and no temperature control on Opus/Sonnet 5.5, so answers are non-deterministic. Many operating facts are unverified ([U]): function bundle limit, Blobs pricing and latency, the dollar value of a compute credit, AI Gateway pass-through, and req.signal behavior. No API call was made, so all latency and quality numbers are estimates.

Blast radius (my inference, not stated in C). On a Free plan the 300-credit limit is a hard limit that pauses the whole site (infra-netlify.md:588). Function compute is 10 credits/GB-h and requests 2 credits per 10k. A bot flood on /api/ask (the site already sees about 18% of views from CN/SG/HK/DE and about 1,900 scanner 404s per 30 d) could exhaust Netlify credits even while the Anthropic cap holds. C prices compute only 'by proxy' [U].

It changes the site's promises. The privacy page says no personal data and the Historian says it runs entirely in the browser, so it needs an opt-in consent flow (D-03) and privacy, terms, banner and guide rewrites. It also puts a generative system in a sensitive domain (Lost Cause framing, period racial language), so a P0 harmful-output incident is a real owner-level burden.

Its curated-answer SEO idea (D-10, pre-generate about 300-400 answers) conflicts with seo-growth.md:369, which says human-written and reviewed only and no bulk LLM generation because it would poison the Historian eval. Retrieval quality still leans on the shared A engine and ingestion work (recall@5 for plain BM25 measured only 6/20 on 20 probes), so C does not avoid A's hardest work.
Reviewer time is about 25-38 h across R2-R3 (about 3k reviews), and the design depends on a volunteer historian for sign-off on contested answers.

judges.recommendation:
Recommended stack: A first and fully, with cheap grafts from B and C at build time. Treat B's runtime tier and C's live-LLM tier as optional, evidence-gated add-ons, and default to neither.

Ranking on cost, sustainability and solo-maintainer burden: A (86), then B (47), then C (44).

Why not B or C by default
- B has a 3.4-point measured ceiling on today's battery and about 33 opt-in users per month at current traffic.
- C's recurring spend floor of about $40-70/month is above its serving cost at today's roughly 110 Historian views per 30 days. It also adds ops burden and a privacy change.
- Caveat on the numbers: the effort totals are not comparable. A's 54-85 d includes ingestion. B's 20-25 d and C's 26-38 d exclude the shared 45-80 d of ingestion.

Stage 0 (about 1-2 weeks, roughly 3-5 d, unblocks everything)
1. Create the Git repo and move to Git/CLI deploys (N1).
2. Ship the H0 hotfix (about 0.5 d).
3. Confirm the Netlify plan and credit balance. It is unverified, and it sizes every cost figure above.
4. Run A's spikes S-1 (.bin compression), S-2 (5,000-file deploy) and S-4 (IA reader index). Run S-3 (real-device latency) once a real phone is available.
5. Graft from B section 8.4 and patch sw.js. The activate handler deletes every cache that is not CACHE_NAME, so change the filter to k.startsWith('gbg-') && k !== CACHE_NAME. Also bypass /hx/ (or /historian/) in the fetch handler. A does not mention this bug, and without the fix A's hx-v<schema> cache would be wiped on the next service-worker bump.
6. Batch releases roughly weekly. Each production deploy is 15 credits, and 20 deploys equal the whole 300-credit Free allowance.

Stage 1: A P0-P1 (about 16-23 d)
- Fixes the Historian on the site's own data. That covers the entity/facts tier, search-core, composers, the redesigned card and the forbidden-string linter.
- This is the first visible win, in about 2-3 weeks of focused work. It costs $0 per query and has no licensing risk.

Stage 2: A P2, the Official Records backbone (8-12 d plus 8-15 h review)
- Delivers page-cited answers and the time-evidence tables that resolve audit C4.
- Graft from B: the T0+ build-time doc2query expansion. It goes in a separate index-only field flagged generated:true, and is excluded from quote spans, citations and the golden set.
- Graft from C section 4.5: Batch-API LLM link proposals fed into the human review queue (about $17-34 for 26k chunks). This cuts reviewer hours. Nothing enters a facts table without human acceptance.
- Estimated one-time LLM spend is about $50-100 (C's estimate).
- Guardrail: seo-growth.md:369 forbids bulk LLM-generated public pages and warns that generated text would poison the eval. So LLM output stays proposals and index-only, and the held-out golden set stays human-authored. Any Q&A pages stay human-written, roughly 60 reviewed questions.
- Add C's may_send_to_llm flag to sources.yaml now. It is cheap today and costly to retrofit, and Tier B and A-pending sources must be false.

Stage 3: A P3-P4, by source family (about 17-28 d, each family stoppable)
- Order: NY/PA/Fox, then B&L, Joint Committee and SHSP shortlist with mandatory perspective tags.
- Cap review at 3-4 h/week and name a historical reviewer.
- Re-tune the gate after every expansion, because canonical@1 and decline both regressed when 299 records were added.

Decision gate G-X at the end of P2, on A's own G150 paraphrase and passage slice
- If A plus T0+ reaches recall@5 of at least 0.80, stop. This is the expected and cheapest outcome, and it is a full success against the goal of greatly expanding the databases.
- If the gap is retrieval (paraphrase recall), run B's 4-day B0 bake-off. Its kill rule is +10 points recall@5 on 60 or more items with a CI excluding 0.
  - Prefer A's own lighter section 7.8(d) reranker gate: model of 8 MB or less, +8 points recall@5, p95 of 150 ms or less on a Moto-G-class phone.
  - Do not build B's roughly 40 MB tier, WebGPU reranker or fine-tune (B5/B6) unless B0 clearly passes.
- If the gap is synthesis, or the owner explicitly wants prose 'why' answers, build a C-lite tier, and only when all of these hold:
  - A's P2 gate has passed, since C reuses the same search-core and KB.
  - The Netlify plan is confirmed and the owner accepts the privacy rewrite.
  - Caps are $25/month and $2/day, with the Anthropic workspace cap at $30. Start with C's 1-2 d R0 spike to replace estimates with measurements, because no API call was made.
  - Ship it opt-in, with the S0 static fallback and a kill switch. Defer C's R3 items (tool route A2, contextual headers, dense fusion) until measured.
  - Ask the owner about Netlify's credit blast radius on the Free plan, a risk C does not model. That point is my inference and is unverified.

Key open questions and unverified items
- Netlify plan and credits, file-count and .bin compression limits, and the function bundle limit are unverified.
- Every phone latency, dense-retrieval quality figure, and all API latency and cost figures for B and C are estimates. Only A's index size, latency and linker precision were actually measured, and even those are Node-on-desktop numbers.
- Whether a named historical reviewer and 1-2 volunteers exist decides whether the review queue is sustainable.

scores.design: A: arch-static-hybrid (static entity/facts tables + sharded BM25 passage index, extractive cited answers, zero server)
strengths: Faithfulness by construction: every answer sentence is (a) template text filled from a fact/entity field, (b) a verbatim quote identified by (passage_id, start, end) and hash-checked, or (c) an explicit limitation (invariants I1-I8, validator V03). No generated text, so no fabricated sentence. The quote-span linter also re-runs in Playwright over the golden run. Numbers are only emitted from fact rows or inside quotations.

Best-evidenced design. Measured on 7 real public-domain sources: 14,391 passages, 3.19M words (288x the 11,088 words indexed today), full inverted index 1.5 MB brotli, BM25 top-10 at 0.057 ms p50 / 0.126 ms p95 in Node, typo repair (Damerau-Levenshtein) 100% recall on 2,682 single-edit typos, and a grammar unit linker that got 24 of 25 hand-checked links right and reaches 389 of 467 regiments versus 45 today. It also caught that a naive alias linker is wrong about 1 time in 3 (7/22).

Answer quality is strongest on what visitors actually ask. Entity, alias and typo repair, intent rules, and fact tables (tenures, stats, rank, rollups) answer who/when/how many/which brigades questions from tables. The prototype ablation shows derived aliases and entity linking are the load-bearing parts (canonical@1 falls 16 without aliases).

Turns audit C4 (clock mismatch) into a feature. Time evidence tables list reported times with page citations, contemporaneous versus retrospective evidence class, and median/range. Times are stored as 1863 clock minutes, never ticks, and legacy map labels are forbidden strings.

Perspective and contested-topic handling is designed in: side/genre/lag chips, a contested registry, and a rule that a contested passage is never shown alone (I6). Known-unknown rules return limited answers ('the records do not give per-location casualty totals') instead of a guess.

UX is zero-friction: no consent step, no privacy-policy change, works offline, 0 bytes added to first paint, worker compute p95 target of 50 ms. Modelled cold first passage answer is about 2.1 s from page load on Slow 4G and 60-150 ms when cached. The answer-first card (one lead plus at most 2 collapsed evidence cards, replacing 2,989-character dumps), citations drawer, filters, scan links and a WCAG 2.2 spec address hist-current UX-01 to UX-18 and audit H8.

Zero per-query cost and no third-party requests (connect-src 'self'), which gives the simplest possible privacy story. The KB, schema, citation contract and eval set are architecture-neutral, so an LLM tier can be added later without re-ingesting.

Most rigorous evaluation and governance for a solo dev: G150 with dev/held-out split, Wilson lower-bound gates, a pinned must-pass list, forbidden-string list, numeric gates per phase, and an honest note that the prototype missed the H2 gates on held-out data. CI tier gate uses a curated identifier allow-list (not 'date <= 1930'), reprint rejection, and a corrections/tombstone workflow.
weaknesses: Cannot synthesise. 'Why', contested, comparative and multi-hop questions get templates plus 1863 official-report prose, not a plain-language explanation. That is a real UX and quality gap for students and casual visitors, and it is where the audit H8 complaint (irrelevant or dumped answers) lived.

Vocabulary gap is addressed only by hypotheses. B's pilot found BM25 recall@5 of 27% on plain-language questions versus 67% on keyword queries (single author with gold in view, so an upper bound on the gap). A's concept lexicon, PMI neighbours and pseudo-relevance feedback measured about 0 on the current battery, and the on-device rerank is deferred to a gated Phase 5.
The passage-recall gate (recall@5 >= 0.80 at P2) is a target. The 175-query battery contains zero passage-gold questions, so the real retrieval baseline does not exist yet.

Heavy human cost: 54-85 person-days plus a unit-link review queue of roughly 300-600 items (8-15 h) for the Official Records alone. Unreviewed links must be worded 'passages that mention...', which weakens unit-specific answers until the queue is worked.

Operational unknowns: Netlify file-count and drag-and-drop limits for 2.7k-3.5k shard files, whether CDN compresses .bin, and plan credits are all unverified [U]. It realistically requires the Git/CLI deploy move (N1).

Phone latency is a x6 model, not a measurement. Adding data shifts the gate (prototype canonical@1 fell 91.4 to 87.9 and correct decline 94.1 to 88.2 after adding 299 records), so thresholds need re-tuning at every corpus growth.

scores.design: B: arch-semantic-local (on-device dense retrieval layered on A: quantised arctic-embed-xs in ORT-Web WASM, RRF fusion, opt-in ~40 MB)
strengths: Only design that measures headroom before committing. Its own analysis shows the ceiling on the existing battery is 6 of 175 queries (3.4 points), and it wraps the whole workstream in a kill criterion: stop unless hybrid beats BM25 by +10 points recall@5 on the paraphrase subset with a paired-bootstrap CI excluding 0 (G-B0). It also honestly notes that a +5-point win is undetectable with about 95 questions (CI about +/-11-13 points).

Privacy by construction: queries, embeddings and clicks never leave the device, connect-src stays 'self', deep links use #q= so the question does not reach Referer or Netlify analytics, and it works offline after opt-in.
Same faithfulness posture as A (extractive, runtime assertion that quote is a substring of the chunk, perspective/sensitivity/controversy flags, 'accounts differ' card). Nothing is generated.

Good evidence quality where it measured: vocabulary-gap pilot on 11,425 real chunks (recall@5 100% / 66.7% / 27.3% for source-wording / keyword / plain question registers), exact int8 scan of 50k x 384 vectors in 11 ms on desktop, verified model and runtime facts (arctic-embed-xs Apache-2.0, 22.97 MB int8, ORT wasm 3.07 MB br), and WebKit storage and 7-day eviction rules.

Highest-value graftable parts even if B is never shipped: T0+ build-time document-expansion field (no runtime ML, flagged generated, never displayed), the sw.js bug findings (activate deletes every cache not named CACHE_NAME at sw.js:24-31; page-level /historian traffic is intercepted), tokenizer/embedding parity tests, pooled 3-system annotation with two annotators and Cohen's kappa, hash deep links, and append-only result refinement (never reorder what the reader is reading).

Understands the classic dense failure: a nearest neighbour always exists, and 27% of the pilot's plain-language questions retrieved only off-topic chunks while still matching words, so a lexical-only gate would answer them. It adds a dense-agreement signal and a scope-exemplar kNN to the gate and calibrates them for decline precision >= 0.95.
weaknesses: Not a standalone answer architecture. It assumes A's interfaces (I1-I8), which its author never saw, and its answer composition is A's extractive composer. It therefore does not fix the synthesis, plain-language or 'why' gap; it only tries to recover more of the right passages.

No neural embedding was run in this study, so every dense-quality claim is a target or a public benchmark. All phone latencies are estimates, and the transformers.js v4 API is unverified. The value is conditional on the future expanded corpus, not on today's data.

Worst UX economics of the three. Only opt-in users benefit, and they must download about 40 MB (27 MB runtime plus 13-21 MB vectors). iOS Safari deletes script-writable storage after 7 days without interaction, so it is a re-buy. There is an enable/warm-up flow and results may change after first render ('More sources found'). At about 110 Historian views a month, roughly 33 people would opt in.
Bandwidth risk: at 10x traffic the opt-in payload consumes about 264 credits a month, or 88% of a Free plan's 300-credit hard limit (plan unverified). It needs a kill switch and a host-move plan.

Added risk surface: 'wasm-unsafe-eval' in the /historian CSP, a dense gate that can wrongly answer out-of-scope questions, and a real cost that is not embeddings but entity/time/perspective review of a much larger corpus.

Effort of 20-25 person-days for core B (29-41 with collections and reranker) for a conditional benefit. Anyone who accepts a server tier can keep vectors function-side (about 15 MB) and avoid the client download entirely, so the on-device model is largely dominated by C for that audience.

scores.design: C: arch-rag-function (router-first RAG: shared search-core, Netlify function calling Claude with native search_result citations, 7-layer grounding, budget and abuse controls)
strengths: Highest answer-quality ceiling: cited plain-language prose (80-180 words, high-school reader), attributed disagreements, time-evidence distributions, perspective and bias attribution, multi-turn via a signed thread token, optional multi-hop tools, and human-reviewed curated answers for the traffic head (about 400 pre-generated with the Batch API for about $6.5, top 100 reviewed).

Router-first design means about 30-40% of questions (decline, deterministic facts) never call the model and are answered in the browser by the same search-core as A. The extractive S0 route reuses the same citation contract when AI is off, the budget is exhausted, the provider refuses, or the verifier fails, so the page never depends on the function to answer.

Strongest grounding stack a generative design can have: pre-LLM sufficiency and scope gate, corpus hygiene, sources-only frozen prompt, native citations whose cited_text is returned verbatim by the API at sentence-block granularity, per-claim deterministic checks D1-D10 (numerals, entities, quote substring, attribution, verbatim clock times, conflict presentation), a sampled/risk-triggered Haiku verifier, and offline gates. Only claims that pass checks are streamed.

Cost and abuse engineering is unusually concrete: $0.0235 per answer (Opus 5.5 warm prefix) or $0.012 (Sonnet 5.5); base monthly $14 / $100 / $840 (Opus) and $7 / $53 / $440 (Sonnet) at 1k / 10k / 100k queries; $25/month hard cap; provider-side workspace limits as the authoritative backstop; self-hosted proof-of-work instead of a third-party CAPTCHA; kill switch and a five-state fallback machine.

Honest-positioning contract that is testable: at least 98% of factual sentences carry a verified citation, badges (AI-written from cited sources / assembled from records, no AI / Reviewed), an evidence line and coverage note computed from tags, no raw-question logging, opt-in feedback, and a quarterly accuracy report. Also a calibrated LLM judge (kappa >= 0.8), 3 runs per question because Opus/Sonnet 5.5 sampling cannot be pinned, and zero-tolerance gates.
weaknesses: Faithfulness is statistical, not structural. Native citations prove a quote is verbatim, not that the sentence is entailed by it. The GA gates are claim-level supported >= 97% and citation precision >= 95%, the verifier is a same-vendor smaller model checking the larger one, sampling variance cannot be controlled, and a shown claim can be retracted after the fact. For a history site the failure mode is a fluent wrong sentence, which A rules out by construction.

No API call was made. Every latency and answer-quality figure is an estimate (first checked claim p50 2.8 s / p95 5.5 s, full answer 6-14 s, cold start 0.35-1.0 s, 1.35 tokens per word, thinking-token share). Refusal false positives on war and slavery content are unmeasured [U]. Function bundle limit, req.signal behaviour, cache-tag header name and AI Gateway pass-through of search_result are unverified.

The dominant risk is retrieval, and retrieval is the same lexical stack as A. Its own probe shows 6/20 recall@5 with plain BM25 and 12/20 with a header field (20 probes, crude segmentation). The LLM can only compose what retrieval supplies, and when it misses it says the library does not say, which is honest but not better than A. Dense fusion and query rewrite are deferred and gated.

UX friction and inconsistency: first-use consent and a privacy-page rewrite (today it says the Historian runs entirely in the browser), 100-600 ms proof-of-work, 2-6 s waits, and the experience flips to records-only when the daily cap or breaker trips. My inference: per-IP-hash buckets of 6 AI questions per 10 minutes could throttle a classroom behind one school network.

Operational burden on a solo dev: 5-6 functions, Blobs with last-write-wins (approximate counters), keys, workspace limits, breaker, audits, weekly reviews. 26-38 person-days on top of shared ingestion, and functions with included_files most likely force the Git/CLI deploy move (my inference).

Its recommended first release (R1, RAG over the site's own records, about 1,060 blocks) adds LLM cost, ops and privacy change for a corpus where A's templates plus quotes already work; the real value only arrives after Official Records ingestion (R2).

judges.recommendation:
VERDICT: Build A as the foundation, add C as an optional opt-in explanation layer on top of A, and treat B as a parts bin (harvest cheap grafts now, run its 4-day gate only if a specific retrieval gap remains). The three designs are not really rivals. C already uses A's engine for its decline, deterministic and fallback routes, and B explicitly sits on A. All three share the same expensive part (source ingestion plus entity, time and perspective linking, 45-80 person-days), and the measured evidence says that part, not the retrieval architecture, buys most of the answer quality. On the requested lens: A wins on faithfulness (by construction) and has the best-measured evidence; C wins on answer quality and reader experience for why/contested/narrative questions but costs faithfulness guarantees, adds latency and consent friction, and rests on estimates because no API call was made; B is the weakest UX and the least proven.

STAGED PLAN

Stage 0 (about 1-2 weeks, no new architecture, prerequisite for everything):
- Ship the hist-current H0 hotfix (undefined and raw ids, hold legacy clock labels).
- Create the historian-data git repo and move to Git/CLI deploys (N1). This helps A (thousands of shard files), and C's functions most likely need it too (my inference).
- Create sources.yaml with the tier gate. Add C's may_send_to_llm flag now (false for Tier B and A-pending) so an LLM tier can never be contaminated later. Use slug source ids to avoid the SRC-01/SRC-19 numbering clash between hist-sources-1 and hist-sources-2.
- Build the G150 golden set with A's dev/held-out discipline, pinned must-pass list and forbidden strings, plus B's pooled labelling from at least 3 systems, two annotators on 30% with kappa >= 0.6, and bootstrap CIs. Add the passage-gold and paraphrase questions the current battery lacks.
- Fix sw.js per B (activate must delete only 'gbg-*' caches, sw.js:24-31) and per A (no skipWaiting/clients.claim/location.reload, audit C6).

Stage 1 = Design A P1: entity plus facts tier, shared search-core, composers, UI v2 on the site's own data. This alone fixes audit H8 (dumped, irrelevant, over-promised answers). Exit on A's P1 gates (S@1 >= 93/90, canonical@1 >= 92, fact@3 >= 90, correct decline >= 92, zero forbidden strings, Lighthouse >= 95).

Stage 2 = Design A P2-P4: Official Records backbone with page citations and time-evidence tables (delivers the C4 fix as a feature), then state books and Fox tables, then participant voices with mandatory perspective tags. This is the 'greatly expanded databases' deliverable. Graft during this stage:
- From C: pre-generated, human-reviewed 'Reviewed answers' (C0) for the top 100-400 questions as static JSON with a named reviewer, disclosed as reviewed and cited (also a 'why/contested' quality lift and an SEO asset for audit T1). Also C's deterministic evidence line and coverage note ('fewer Confederate regimental sources are in the library yet'), and A's sentence-boundary offsets (sb) used as C's citable blocks so C can plug in later without re-ingesting.
- From B: T0+ build-time expansion field (generated:true, never displayed or quoted) only if the G150 shows a paraphrase recall shortfall; the golden-set method; hash-based #q= deep links instead of ?q=; append-only refinement (never reorder a visible answer); tokenizer parity discipline if any model is ever added.

DECISION GATE G1 (after A P2, on the held-out G150): if passage recall@5 >= 0.80, citation precision >= 0.90 and residual failures are mostly synthesis/plain-language rather than misses, proceed to Stage 3. If recall@5 is below 0.80 on the paraphrase subset, do T0+ expansion first, then consider Stage 4.

Stage 3 (optional, opt-in, gated) = Design C as a per-query button, not a global mode. A's answer renders instantly and remains the default. Under it a button 'Explain these sources in plain language (AI)' sends the same retrieved passages to the function. This avoids a blocking consent modal, makes cost and consent per action, keeps A's extractive card as the S0 fallback, and puts the user's eyes on cited sources first.
- Run C's R0 spike (1-2 days) early, in parallel with A P2, to replace the estimates (latency, tokens per word, refusal behaviour on war and slavery content, streaming plus citations plus fallbacks, bundle and Blobs limits).
- Skip C's R1 (own-records-only) as a separate release; go straight to a C R2-lite on A's index: function, proof-of-work, rate/budget/breaker/kill switch, in-stream checks D1-D10, S0 fallback. Incremental effort is roughly 19-29 person-days (C's 26-38 minus R1's 7-9; my arithmetic).
- Ship only if: claim-level supported >= 97%, unsupported numerals/dates/names = 0 in CI, citation precision >= 95%, adversarial suite 100%, over-refusal <= 8%, and the privacy page, Terms and Historian banner are rewritten first. Suggested caps: $25/month, $2/day. Model choice (Opus 5.5 vs Sonnet 5.5 vs Haiku 4.5 per route) is the owner's decision (D-01) via C's bake-off.
- Keep two labelled modes: 'Records only' (default, on-device) and 'AI explanation (beta)'. Do not use 'AI-style' or 'runs entirely in your browser' copy.

Stage 4 (only if a gap remains): B, minimally. Run B0 (4 days) only if G1 shows the paraphrase gap persists after T0+ and either (a) the owner rejects server AI on privacy grounds or (b) offline semantic search is wanted. If C is live, prefer function-side vectors (about 15 MB, no client download) over shipping a model to phones. Ship B's client model only if it clears +10 points recall@5 on the paraphrase subset with a 95% paired-bootstrap CI excluding 0. Do not pursue B5/B6 (cross-encoder, fine-tune).

INTEGRATION CONFLICTS TO SETTLE BEFORE ANY CODE
1. URL prefix: A uses /hx/, B uses /historian/, C uses /data/historian/. Choose one outside /data/ (recommend /hx/), because /data/* is max-age=3600 and sw.js caches it network-first (sw.js:61).
2. Service worker: A wants cache-first for /hx/*, B wants the SW to bypass /historian/*. Recommendation: cache-first under its own 'hx-' cache name with the activate purge limited to 'gbg-*'.
3. Passage ids: adopt A's content-hash ids plus append-only numeric map; A's sb offsets serve as C's citable blocks.
4. Deep links: use #q= (B) rather than ?q= (A, C).
5. Copy: A says 'records only, not AI', C says 'AI-assisted'. Present two explicit modes, default Records.

CAVEATS ON THIS JUDGEMENT
- I scored the design documents, not running systems. I did not re-run any script or re-verify vendor facts (models, prices, Netlify limits) cited by the architects.
- A's measurements are the strongest; B's dense-quality numbers are targets and C's latency and quality numbers are estimates.
- Scores would swing toward C if the owner values plain-language synthesis above by-construction faithfulness and accepts the consent, ops and cost trade-offs. Traffic is small (about 110 Historian views a month), so C's dollar cost is trivial while its complexity and privacy change are not.

final.summary:
Verdict: build Design A (records-only static hybrid: entity + facts tier, sharded BM25 passage index, verbatim page-cited quotes, time-evidence tables, perspective chips, honest refusals) as the permanent core. It is the only design measured on real text (14,391 passages / 3,192,212 words from 7 sources, 1.54 MB brotli index, 0.057 ms p50 BM25 in Node; I re-counted the words) and costs $0 per query with zero third-party requests. Graft two build-time-only ideas: B's T0+ document-expansion field (index-only, generated:true, never displayed or cited) and C's Batch-API link proposals into the human review queue (about $31-61 total, cap $75, Tier A sources only via a may_send_to_llm flag). B (on-device semantic search, about 40 MB opt-in) and C (per-click 'Explain these sources (AI, beta)') are optional, default-OFF branches decided at one gate G-X at the end of Phase 2: if paraphrase-slice recall@5 >= 0.80 with T0+, the architecture is frozen (expected); if not, cheap levers, then an 8 MB reranker experiment (+8 pts, p95 <= 150 ms), then B0 (+10 pts, CI excludes 0); C-lite only if the residual is synthesis, the Netlify plan is confirmed, privacy pages are rewritten first, caps are $25/month and $2/day, and C's R0 spike replaces estimates.

Database growth: from 658 records / 11,088 indexed words / 0 page citations to about 22-27 k passages / 4.4-5.4 M words by end of P4 (24-29 k / 5-6 M with the P5 base), i.e. roughly 400-540x, plus 957+ entity cards, 9 fact tables, a 137-event time-evidence table (the audit C4 deliverable), about 60 reviewed answers and static SEO unit pages. Index 2.4-3.1 MB br, text 11-14 MB br, T1 <= 250 KB, 0 bytes added to first paint. Source order: OR vol. 27 pts 1-3 (7.4 k passages, 589 reports, dispatches) -> NY Final Report x3 + PA 1914 + Fox/Guild casualty facts + ME/NJ/MI/MN -> Battles & Leaders v3, Joint Committee, SHSP shortlist (~150 articles), memoirs with mandatory perspective/bias tags -> regiment histories, civilians/press -> gated rosters (CWSS, blocked until NPS confirms in writing), Wikipedia/OSM/photos. Full licensing/attribution table, retro-audit of 18 shipped Tier B/C-derived monument coordinates, slug-based source ids, and unified schema (source/document/passage with sentence blocks/entity/9 fact tables/anchor/manifest/answer/golden records) are in the report.

Key decisions and corrections to the inputs: /hx/ URL prefix (never /data/); sw.js patch (activate purge limited to gbg-*, bypass /hx/, remove skipWaiting/reload) verified at sw.js:24-31,61-70; deep links use the URL fragment (#q=) so questions never reach analytics; golden sets merged into Golden-Core (hist-golden-set.json, 150, 100 dev/50 locked, baselines B0 14.0%, B3 29.3%) plus new Golden-Passage (about 105 at P2, 155 at P4) because the existing set has no passage-gold items; Design A's '4-6 months at 15 h/week' does not compute (54-85 days is 29-45 weeks) and is recomputed; Judge 2's 19-29 d C-lite estimate is revised to 15-29 d because C's R1 plumbing cannot be skipped; no bulk LLM-generated public answers (seo-growth-23 forbids it). UI spec covers desktop (side Sources panel >= 900 px) and mobile (bottom sheet, 44 px targets, safe-area input bar, stacked evidence tables <= 480 px, landscape rules), WCAG 2.2 AA, CWV budgets (LCP <= 1.5 s, CLS <= 0.05, INP <= 200 ms, Lighthouse >= 95 mobile and desktop), and a 10-viewport acceptance matrix. Evaluation gates are consolidated per phase (always-gates: injection 100%, forbidden content 0, hallucinated citations 0; battery S@1 >= 93/90 at P1; passage recall@5 >= 0.80/0.85/0.90; citation precision >= 0.90/0.92/0.95; A+ Golden-Core pass >= 95%, locked >= 93%). Effort: core (P0-P4 + governance) 49-76 person-days, 57-90 with the P5 base, optional B0 4 d, optional C-lite 15-29 d; reviewer time 59-95 h (3-4 h/week); calendar 26-40 weeks at 15 h/week for the core. Unverified: Netlify plan/credits, file-count and .bin compression limits, all phone latencies and all B/C quality and API latency/cost numbers (no embedding run, no API call made); the Free-plan credit-exhaustion blast radius of a function flood is my inference.

eval.summary:
Deliverables: (1) C:/Users/mlege/AppData/Roaming/Claude/scratch-workspaces/fe20000a-2144-4d85-ac4c-4e19e62f5823/1fb796a8-22ef-47aa-b6e3-227d4048a221/scratch-2026-09-30-719300/plan-work/hist-golden-set.json (150 questions, 17 categories, fields id/category/question/expected_answer_points/expected_source_ids/answerable_now/needs_source/difficulty plus data_status, phase_ready, must_not_match, anchors, truth_basis, split, etc.); (2) plan-work/hist-eval.md (metrics, scoring rubric, human review protocol, regression gates, CI how-to, baselines, appendices with sign-off queue and all 150 questions). Working tools (dependency-free Node) in plan-work/tmp-hist-golden/: build-golden.js, verify-golden.js, score-golden.js, run-system.js, run-baselines.js, pr-comment.js, gates.json, spec/, golden.jsonl.

Composition: 150 questions = unit facts 12, commander 10, casualties 10, place/terrain 9, timing/sequence 9, cause/effect/controversy 9, ancestor/regiment lookup 8, comparison 8, quotes 8, on-site 8, classroom 7, misspellings/aliases/abbreviations 10, multi-hop 9, temporal "at 3pm on July 2" 8, out-of-scope 10, adversarial/prompt-injection 8, ambiguous 7. 113 answerable now from DEPLOY_DIR/data (88 data-backed + 25 behaviour probes); 37 mark needs_source and name the source type (28 need expanded sources by hist-sources-1/2 catalog id, 9 need the canonical time model). Phase readiness H1 40 / H2 83 / H3 27. Split: 100 dev, 50 locked. Zero exact overlap with hist-current's 118+57 batteries.

Verification: every current-data anchor (record id plus key fact, or a computed aggregate such as argmax/count/sum, ambiguity candidate counts, clock-to-tick mapping) is evaluated against the deployed data at build time and the build aborts on any failure; verify-golden.js re-checks from the JSON alone plus a data fingerprint. 349/349 anchors pass; a deliberate mutation (20th Maine strength 386 to 387) is caught with exit code 2 naming the item. Build also proves every point is satisfiable by its own example and that no forbidden pattern fires on the golden text.

Baselines measured with the shipped scorer (n=150): deployed historian.html (B0) passes 14.0% (critical-fact recall 51.7%, 48.7% of answers carry hard render defects, out-of-scope decline 20%, injection/false-premise 0/8, mean answer 3,999 chars); hist-current prototype with unused site data (B3) 29.3%; decline-everything null 6.0%; oracle 100% (bounds the metric). Gates proposed in gates.json: six always-on hard gates (injection/XSS/leak 100%, zero forbidden content, zero hard defects, zero hallucinated citations, OOS decline >=90%, false decline <=5%), H1/H2/H3 and A+ gates aligned to hist-current section 9 and qa-ci HC-06/07/09, 2-point regression tolerance.

Findings surfaced while authoring (encoded as tests): the site's Confederate corps rows sum to 21,500 vs the army row 28,000; casualty_apportionment says C-26NC has the highest Confederate rate but C-8VA (76.7%), C-38NC-S and C-9VA exceed it in the OOB; U-I-3-1 and U-I-3-2 both list Roy Stone as commander; D3T525 vs V-015 misorder Alexander's two notes; V-001 'Alphonso Hodges' vs 'Alpheus Hodges' in time-facts; NY has 75 site records vs 68 infantry + 19 batteries in the NY Final Report; chronology labels put 'Garnett reaches the wall' at noon; terrain LOC-006 does carry 'Nearly 6,000 casualties' (corrects hist-current 2.5 #8, which said no per-location totals exist). 19 items (17 shape-only, 2 author-recall: Biddle, Sherfy) cannot be locked until a historian signs off; 13 more inherit time-facts confidence limits; 7 controversy items need framing review.
